blocks.text: People getting voting info from AI an ‘emerging concern’, AEC says

blocks.caption: Josh Taylor

blocks.text: Josh Taylor

The Australian Electoral Commissioner, Jeff Pope, has said people getting their information about voting in Australia from AI chatbots such as ChatGPT or Claude is an “emerging concern”, and has forced the commission to overhaul its website to attract bots looking for the correct information.

Speaking at a hearing of the joint standing committee on artificial intelligence on Wednesday night, Pope said it was “dangerous” to rely on social media platforms or AI tools as “your only source of research when it comes to forming an opinion around voting” and was something the AEC was working to educate the public on.
He said it may require a legislative response from parliament in terms of what platforms and and cannot do in terms of the content on their platforms around elections.
Pope pointed to a study on the Scottish election reported by The Guardian in May found that AI services gave voters misinformation to 34% of the questions it posed.
The AEC had started to prepare for this, he said.

double quotation markWe’re undertaking significant investment at the moment in modernising our web page so that AI tools actually pull factual information from our web page and reflect that back to the voter, rather than pulling ... from a variety of other resources which may or may not be correct.
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, has disputed the trade minister’s claims he walked out of a meeting on the European Union trade deal, suggesting Don Farrell might be “under a lot of pressure”.
Farrell told the ABC yesterday afternoon that Canavan and shadow foreign affairs minister, Ted O’Brien, had walked out on him while he was explaining the deal.
In response, Canavan said:

double quotation markI can understand that Don is under a lot of pressure, because there are barely any friends of his dud European deal. I am happy to meet with Don anytime, but he ended our discussion, not me. I have written to Don with practical suggestions about how the deal can be improved and I remain open to discuss my concerns at any time.

While the deal has been agreed to between Australian and EU representatives, it still requires support from parliament. The Coalition has already ruled out its support while the Greens are considering the details before revealing their final position.
Anika Wells to introduce digital duty of care bill today

blocks.caption: Josh Butler

blocks.text: Josh Butler
Anika Wells will introduce the government’s digital duty of care bill into the parliament today, with all eyes on what amendments Labor may have made to the initial draft bill.
The communications minister has confirmed the government will drop its earlier plans for her office to have broad rule-making powers to define what content is classed as “harmful”.
According to excerpts of her National Press Club speech, to be delivered at 12.30pm today, Wells will say:

double quotation markIn response to concerns we heard during the exposure draft consultation and to make this abundantly clear, we have removed the ministerial rule-making power to define new harms in the final bill.
Instead, new “harms” will be added by parliament through legislative amendment.
Wells will tell the NPC that the digital duty of care will “set basic safety standards for the online services we use every day, just like we have in every other industry”.

double quotation markWe must shift the burden from the shoulders of victims to the companies that are creating the environments where harms occur. The Digital Duty of Care gives Australians choice... If someone wants their feed filled with friends and creators they follow, the social media platforms must give them that choice. And if you’re happy to stick with your algorithm – you can do so.
Wells will also confirm new carve-outs for journalists and news media in the Online Safety Act, to assist professional news organisations and public interest journalism.
We’ll bring you more from her speech later in the day.
Victorian Labor pledges to offer free abortion care

blocks.caption: Benita Kolovos

blocks.text: Benita Kolovos
The Victorian Labor government will today announce that – if re-elected in November – they will make Victoria the first state to offer free abortion care.

Under the $30m election commitment, the government would pay private providers to deliver medical and surgical abortions up to 16 weeks, removing out-of-pocket costs. This means women would no longer need to pay for GP or specialist consultations, imaging and tests or medications at participating providers.

Medical abortions can cost almost $700 out of pocket for patients with a Medicare card, or more than $1,000 for those without one. Surgical abortions can cost $895 with Medicare, rising to almost $1,500 for those without a card.

The government has also committed to extending the window for medical abortion from nine to 10 weeks’ gestation. If elected, they would direct Safer Care Victoria to lead a clinical review into extending access to the medication up to 12 weeks, which aligns with World Health Organisation guidelines. The review would also cover who should be able to deliver care and where.

Patients who need to travel to access abortion would also be eligible for a subsidy to help with their travel and accommodation costs, community health care providers trained to provide abortion care and 1800 My Options would receive extra funding under the plan.
The health minister, Ingrid Stitt, said this morning:
double quotation markAbortion care is healthcare and Labor will make it free. Only Labor will protect a woman’s right to choose.
Albanese to attack Hanson over 'monoculture' remarks

blocks.caption: Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: Sarah Basford Canales
Anthony Albanese will criticise Pauline Hanson’s claim that Australia should be “monocultural”, suggesting that anyone who believes that “should get themselves down to the nearest Specsavers”.
In a speech , the prime minister will say each cultural and ethnic community added to Australia gives the country’s character more “breadth”, expands “palates” and unites people.

double quotation markAustralia’s migration story has been many generations in the making. Anyone who can look in the rear-vision mirror and see a monoculture should get themselves down to the nearest Specsavers. The reality is that Australia’s heart is multicultural.

His speech at the conference for the Federation of Ethnic Communities Councils of Australia will also encourage people of different cultures to celebrate with one another while embracing an Australian identity.
He will say:

double quotation markI want every Australian to be able to add to our country, and to feel proud of what they bring. I want every Australian to leave behind the baseline of mere tolerance for something far greater: the joy of celebration ... Celebrating the birthright of heritage and the comforts and strengths of faith. Celebrating the land of your roots while adding to the land that is your home, and your future.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

articles.title: Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and extreme comments
articles.summary:
Party faces fresh crisis as three councillors quit after ITV undercover filming exposed violence, misogyny and racist views

Reform UK has been rocked by a fresh crisis after councillors and…

blocks.text: Reform UK has been rocked by a fresh crisis after councillors and election candidates for the party were caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.
Three councillors have already stood down from the party, which said it was conducting an investigation over the first revelations from an ITV undercover investigation that aired on Wednesday.

Reform leader Nigel Farage has postponed a major announcement that was due to take place in Essex on Thursday morning as the party tries to contain the fallout expected to come from further revelations in the coming days. That will include revelations from undercover filming of senior Reform politicians and officials working at its UK headquarters.

Farage has made repeated pledges over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.

However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites,” and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.
Feeney won seats on Birmingham city council and Solihull Metropolitan borough council and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. He has announced that he has left Reform “for personal reasons”.

Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues.

Feeney was filmed with other candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, talking about where a local mosque might be built. After they make extreme racist comments in the discussion, Feeney says: “Oh god, we’re all going to end up in the papers”.
Chris Whelan announced he had resigned from Reform on 12 October “on personal and health grounds”. Campbell is still in post.

Dean Miller, a Reform councillor for Bromley, was filmed separately making a range of comments during campaigning for the Makerfield byelection, including when he discussed what he would do with illegal immigrants crossing the Channel.
after newsletter promotion
Reform has been attempting to pre-empt the impact from the ITV investigation, which will potentially be at its most damaging when footage from inside Reform’s London HQ airs.
The party used a statement issued on Wednesday night to accuse ITV and Hardcash Productions of “extreme methods of deception”.

“They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees,” it said.

The party said that this came at a time when Farage and other members of Reform were “being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation”.

“They have not included this in their report, despite being on notice since March this year. There is currently an ongoing police investigation relating to security breaches against Mr Farage, as is well known,” it added.

Reform said that not all individuals covertly recorded by ITV are members of Reform UK, adding: “Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced. In some cases, there have been suspensions and due process must be followed.”

The latest crisis to hit the party comes at a time when it has been stalling in the polls and faces problems including the fallout from a different undercover investigation which filmed senior officials discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party.
The outcome is also awaited of a parliamentary standards commissioner investigation into whether Farage should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.

Bridget Phillipson MP, chair of the Labour party, said: “The extreme racism and appalling behaviour exposed by this investigation is truly sickening. Nigel Farage can’t shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples. Every Reform councillor, council candidate or party member found to have made such despicable comments must be thrown out of Reform UK immediately.”
Undercover: A Year In Reform, airs on 18 October at 10.20pm on ITV1, ITVX, STV & STV Player.

articles.title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access
articles.summary:
Ukrainian president accused US president of picking the other side over four years of war

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Jessica Elgot Andrew Rothin Kyiv

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv.

The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by the US agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow.

Ahead of a meeting with prime minister Andy Burnham in Downing St, Zelenskyy appeared in a TV interview where he was asked whether the sudden restriction of Starlink was deliberate and if he felt betrayed by Trump.

“Really, yes … but it’s a little bit more complicated ⁠than just my emotions or my feelings,” the Ukrainian president replied, adding: “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner.”

Overnight Ukraine’s military reported that, without explanation, the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph.

That effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable – and, it later emerged, affected the most effective air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv.

“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … Of course, people will die.”

The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.

Trump denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR aired on Wednesday that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.

The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz after the US-Israel attack on Iran has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.

The two leaders fell out in the spring of 2025 during a disastrous visit by Zelenskyy to the Oval Office, where the US president said: “You don’t have the cards” to win the war. The row was followed by a brief pause in intelligence sharing and a desperate scramble by European allies to calm the row.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham greeted Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warmly at No 10. Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters

blocks.text: Burnham met Zelenskyy in Downing Street on Wednesday, hours after he promised MPs that the Ukrainian president “would not leave empty handed” and that he had tasked officials with drawing up further sanctions and options for speeding up military aid.

As the pair met at Number 10, he promised that Britain’s support for Ukraine would remain constant. “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change,” he said.
Zelenskyy had met with King Charles in Buckingham Palace earlier on Wednesday.
In brief remarks to reporters, Zelenskyy said he hoped to raise access to Starlink and intelligence sharing in his meeting with the British prime minister.

Burnham pledged that he will accelerate the supply of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which the country uses to counter Russian drone strikes and said they were looking for “all possible avenues” of further support.
The prime minister also said he was prepared to discuss the ceasefire proposed by Trump on attacks on energy infrastructure but acknowledged that Moscow had not abided by it.
“Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.

Earlier Burnham told MPs at PMQs that he wanted to be “careful” about potential criticism of Trump that might risk exacerbating tensions, saying he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation: “I will listen to President Zelenskyy carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.”

The meeting, which lasted just over an hour, began as Burnham greeted Zelenskyy with a hug on Downing Street, before the pair walked to the door of No 10 and posed for photographs, flanked by Irish guards in full ceremonial uniform.

Musk said that the decision to curtail Starlink was not one made by him. The communications system is not directly licensed to clients who are using weapons, and the Ukrainian military was linked to a related network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Trump.

Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser on military technology to Zelenskyy, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”

Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.

“With their actions our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.

It also complicates Ukraine’s use of medium range, mid strike drones for hitting targets in its territories occupied by Russia. But, ironically, it would have no impact on Ukraine’s deep strike bombing of oil refineries because Kyiv is banned from using Starlink to hit targets inside of Russia.

Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become more widespread.

Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”

articles.title: Kelly Clarkson bird saga takes another turn as store owner's footage is released
articles.summary: Kelly Clarkson's feud with a Brooklyn shop over a singing mechanical bird just got a lot more expensive —15 million dollars more, to be precise.

image.caption: Kelly Clarkson performs on NBC's Today show at Rockefeller Plaza in May 2025, in New York. (Charles Sykes/Invision/Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Kelly Clarkson's feud with a Brooklyn shop over a singing mechanical bird just got a lot more expensive —15 million dollars more, to be precise.
Art of Play store owner ups price to $15 million US
Kelly Clarkson's feud with a Brooklyn shop over a mechanical bird just got a lot more expensive — $15 million more, to be precise.

Adam Rubin, the co-owner of Art of Play, chose to put the shop's automated bird, "Molly," up for sale for a whopping $15 million US amid the shop's ongoing viral feud with the pop star, according to USA Today.
The listing in the store now reads: "Molly. Designed and created by Bliss Kolb. The world's most famous singing bird automata! $15,000,000."
Rubin also told USA Today he'd give each shop employee $15,000 US and pay Kolb $1 million US if someone bought the bird. He said he'd use the rest of the money to buy other antique automata.
CBC News has reached out to Art of Play for confirmation but has not heard back.
It's the latest turn in a saga that has taken over the internet. It's also a dramatic increase from the $15,000 US price tag Clarkson says she saw when she stopped by the store on Oct. 10.
'Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger': shop owner

The shop owner spoke to several outlets at the Art of Play on Tuesday, saying the store has seen a large increase in foot traffic because of the publicity, but has also received a torrent of backlash from fans of the pop star.
"Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger," Rubin said. "We're concerned on behalf of our shopkeepers."
Clarkson's viral shopping experience can now be seen in footage obtained by independent journalist Pablo Torre on Tuesday, Oct. 13.

The four-minute, 50-second clip does not include audio. In it, Clarkson appears to enter the store wearing a baseball cap and a yellow T-shirt. She browses the store and appears to approach a clerk, who says something to her before walking away.
Later on in the video, Clarkson appears to put the items she had in her hands back on the shelves and speak to the person at the cash register before leaving the store.
How we got here
The online spat started on Saturday, when the singer posted that she visited the shop to buy "a few things," but "was looked at as if I couldn't afford it."
"But y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she wrote.
For context, Robert's character in the film is famously treated rudely by a snooty saleswoman in a boutique.
The store replied Sunday, stating that Clarkson had asked about buying "Molly," a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton which is "permanently attached to the wall and isn't for sale."
They said that Clarkson's version of events "would resonate with anyone who has ever felt judged," but said that all shoppers at Art of Play "are equally welcome."
"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," the shop wrote on Instagram.
Clarkson hit back later that day, posting a photo showing a $15,000 US price tag on the wall next to the wooden bird automaton.
"So you're not only rude, you're also a liar. [...] It's not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you, my friend, were an exception," the star wrote.

items: Kelly Clarkson is feuding with a Brooklyn store over alleged 'Pretty Woman' treatment

blocks.text: Clarkson rarely makes personal posts on social media. Her previous post on X was two weeks earlier and promoted her coaching gig on NBC's The Voice.
On Monday, the shop said it told Clarkson the $15,000 US price referred to a nearly identical bird that could be made and sold, not Molly itself.
The store also said it offered to show Clarkson a different bird atomaton on sale for about $2,000 US, but that she didn't stick around long enough to see it.

In an interview with several outlets , Rubin said no one in the shop recognized Clarkson at the time, the store was "packed" and Clarkson was there for "less than five minutes." He also alleged that Clarkson scolded an employee.
"Everybody has a bad day. But things changed when she used her platform to attack us. It's asymmetrical social warfare," he said.
The internet weighs in
On social media, users have been closely following the online debacle and sharing their thoughts.
"This kelly clarkson situation is why everyone should work a retail job at some point in their life bc after u do u will never again care how store employees treat u," one user wrote on X

"Even if you buy kelly clarkson's entire narrative here... this doesn't feel like a pretty woman situation," wrote another, adding that "it seems perfectly reasonable that whoever she spoke to would not really be focused on selling it / expect to."
Molly, a singing and dancing mechanical bird, by Bliss Kolb, is displayed at Art of Play, on Tuesday, in the Brooklyn borough of New York. (Yuki Iwamura/The Associated Press)

"I think the funniest part about this situation is that for anyone to take a side they must either feel empathy for multimillionaire celebrity Kelly Clarkson or these multimillionaire shop owners," a third wrote.

"What we can learn from Kelly Clarkson and Art of Play situation is if any customer asks for a price of your product, the right thing to do is not discriminate based on how they're dressed," another wrote.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca
With files from CBC's Alexandra Mae Jones

articles.title: Farm Boy, L'Ancêtre and Life Smart organic cheeses recalled for possible Listeria contamination
articles.summary: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency is recalling several organic cheese products under the Farm Boy, L'Ancêtre, and Life Smart brands due to possible Listeria contamination.

image.caption: Some Farm Boy organic cheeses are being recalled across Canada, along with organic cheese products from L'Ancêtre and Life Smart. (Canadian Food Inspection Agency)

blocks.text: Canada·New
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency is recalling several organic cheese products under the Farm Boy, L'Ancêtre, and Life Smart brands due to possible Listeria contamination.
CFIA says recall was triggered by testing; no reported illnesses connected to affected products
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) is recalling several organic cheese products under the Farm Boy, L'Ancêtre, and Life Smart brands due to possible Listeria contamination.
The agency says the national recall was triggered by testing and there have been no reported illnesses connected to consumption of the products.
The affected products include Farm Boy organic Swiss, medium cheddar, old cheddar, extra sharp and three-year-old cheddar cheeses with a best before date of July 30, 2027.

Life Smart organic part skim mozzarella cheese with a best before date of March 30, 2027, is also being recalled, as are several shredded organic cheeses made by L'Ancêtre with best before dates of this December, next January and next July.
L'Ancetre's organic Swiss cheese with a best before date of July 30, 2027, is also included.
A full list of the recalled products can be found here. They were sold in stores across the country.
Are food recalls in Canada becoming more common?

The CFIA says people should not consume the product if they have it in their home, and to throw it out or return it to wherever they bought it. It warns that products that look and smell normal can still make someone sick.

Symptoms of Listeria include vomiting, nausea, persistent fever, muscle aches, severe headache and neck stiffness. Pregnant women, the elderly and those with weakened immune systems are at greater risk.
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: Israel blocks construction of key Gaza base created by Trump peace board
articles.summary:
Source tells Guardian Israel has not permitted US-led project to house 150 international troops to move forward

Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s…

blocks.text: Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned.

In early August, the Board of Peace, the international organization authorized in 2025 by the UN and chaired by the US president, issued its first construction contract for Gaza: Louisiana-based Arkel International would construct a military outpost for 150 international troops that would be the vanguard of an international stabilization force.

Two months later, Israel has still not permitted the contract to move forward, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. Contractors and trucks are not being allowed to cross into Gaza and begin the work. “Israel won’t open the border,” they said.
A Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment. Neither the Israeli Defense Forces nor the Israeli government responded to requests for comment.

Israel’s war in Gaza is one of the eight wars Trump claims to have resolved. He listed it again last week in a screed on social media, protesting that it was unfair he had not won the Nobel peace prize.
The Board of Peace, formed in the wake of an October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, is central to Trump’s claims to have ended the conflict.

Arkel’s planned “mission support site temporary outpost” is decidedly rudimentary: a fortified position of about 100 meters by 100 meters, at a site that was once part of the controversial and now defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, according to the person familiar with the matter. The US-backed GHF operated in Gaza from May 2025 till October 2025 to deliver aid protected by private contractors.
The base would host short rotating deployments of a well-armed force of 150 troops in Gaza, the person said. They would come from a larger component of 500 sent already from Morocco and Kosovo.

But without this contract, the source said, the rest of the Board of Peace program cannot launch. Israel’s refusal to allow Arkel, the contractor, to build the base, essentially cuts the Board of Peace off at the legs.

“You can’t get in without [an international stabilization force (ISF)]. You can’t rebuild,” the person said. “There’s no security. There’s no deliveries of construction equipment. You can’t even start putting utilities. You can’t start putting in basic life-support facilities you know because without the ISF you can’t go in.”
The person familiar with the matter said the Board of Peace believes that Israel’s government will let the project proceed after the Israeli elections, which are scheduled for 27 October.

The controversial Board of Peace has a unique structure. Trump is designated as chair for life. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, is an executive board member, as is real estate developer Steve Witkoff, who Trump has appointed as a mediator in various international disputes.
after newsletter promotion

Though many western democracies have kept their distance from the Board of Peace, 28 countries joined as founding members earlier this year. Kushner has unveiled renderings of a futuristic vision of Gaza, where the city was envisioned as a pristine luxury waterfront resort city with hi-tech skyscrapers looking out over the Mediterranean.
On 23 September the group unveiled what it said was a six-month, $2.45bn plan, as the first step towards reconstruction with a 10-year estimated cost of $71bn.
There were lofty promises and requests for contributions. “Today we can point to real progress,” announced Witkoff.

A US senior adviser to the board, Aryeh Lightstone, announced a new fund would be started. “Your high net-worth donations will go directly to the Palestinian people,” he said. Lightstone has traveled in Trump circles since the president’s first term. He officiated as a rabbi at the 2020 wedding of Trump adviser Stephen Miller to Katie Miller.
Israel has continued strikes in Gaza since the October ceasefire, killing approximately 1,400 people over that time, according to Gaza health authorities.

articles.title: OpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annually
articles.summary:
Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares last year

OpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average…

blocks.text: OpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.

Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.

The earnings amount to 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings, according to the Office for National Statistics. An OpenAI worker on an average package could expect to take home about £1,000 an hour in salary and equity before tax.

But there is understood to be a wide discrepancy between the highest and lowest earners. The biggest compensation packages are reserved for AI researchers who help build the San Francisco company’s cutting-edge models such as Astra.
The figures relate to 2025, when there was a talent war and OpenAI’s rival, Meta, was reported to be offering multi-year packages running into several hundred million dollars.

OpenAI’s London base reflects the UK capital’s status as an important hub for AI talent with some of the brightest machine-learning experts and AI researchers coming out of universities such as Cambridge. Google DeepMind is also based in King’s Cross.

The company declined to comment on the figures, which come after a series of AI safety crises involving its models. This summer AI agents, under training, escaped and hacked into an unrelated company website, Hugging Face, while this month one of its safety leaders quit, saying that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.

OpenAI’s London office has been established as its largest international research hub but it also houses a government affairs team and sales and marketing functions – responsible for selling licences to companies and organisations. George Osborne, the former Conservative chancellor of the exchequer, joined last December as the company’s head for countries.
The earnings were a big jump on the previous year, when the average pay and equity package was £1.1m.

Booming AI salaries have already had a significant effect on housing prices in San Francisco, where the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 per month, a figure that is up more than 25% from last year and is nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.
In London, OpenAI UK Ltd recorded a more than trebling of its turnover in 2025 to £293m, on which it made a £20.3m profit.

articles.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story
articles.summary:
Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers

The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to…

blocks.text: The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”

Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.

Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.
She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”
Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.

“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”

blocks.caption: Journalist Vauhini Vara said she had run Kundizeza’s story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost entirely AI generated. Photograph: Andrew Altschul

blocks.text: Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.

Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”
Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.

Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.
“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”
Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.

In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”

Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

articles.title: In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
articles.summary:
Throttling of mobile internet system will affect Kyiv’s air defences more than its strikes on oil refineries. Now Zelenskyy must be hoping that US intel holds

In Ukraine the situation was…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

blocks.text: In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.

Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.

Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).
Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.

blocks.caption: The aftermath of a Russian missile attack in Kyiv on Wednesday. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

blocks.text: The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia.

However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.

Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”

However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.
So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.

The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.
“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.
A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.

Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.
after newsletter promotion

The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.

Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.

“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.

Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.

The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.

As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”

Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.

articles.title: Ottawa to announce over $350M for skilled trades worker training, recruitment
articles.summary: The federal government will announce plans to help fund new infrastructure, equipment and recruitment efforts by unions and other organizations to train workers as part of a major funding…

image.caption: Secretary of State for Labour John Zerucelli is expected to make the funding announcement on Thursday. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The federal government will announce plans to help fund new infrastructure, equipment and recruitment efforts by unions and other organizations to train workers as part of a major funding announcement expected on Thursday.
Funding part of effort to hire and train 80,000 to 100,000 new workers by 2031
Secretary of State for Labour John Zerucelli is expected to announce more than $350 million in funding, according to a senior government official speaking on background.
CBC News is not naming the official because they were not authorized to discuss the details of the announcement.

The funding aims to help fulfil an objective announced in the spring economic update called Team Canada Strong — a plan to recruit, train and hire 80,000 to 100,000 new skilled trades workers with the nationally recognized Red Seal certification by 2030-31.

The push is part of an ongoing effort to close a gap of more than 20,000 skilled trades workers per year. It comes as the Liberals' C-39, a bill intended to speed up major project approvals and construction, moves through Parliament.

The funding will be provided partially through the Union Training and Innovation Program (UTIP) and partially through the money earmarked in the spring economic update, and will include three different streams.

items: Carney government proposes $6B to hire 100,000 new skilled trades workers

blocks.text: The first stream will help fund investments in equipment for unions, colleges and other organizations that train workers in the Red Seal trades. The federal government will temporarily pay up to 70 per cent of the cost of training equipment, up from 50 per cent.

The second stream, infrastructure, is intended to help unions and organizations training workers expand or build union-run training centres to increase capacity across the country. The government is looking to help finance shovel-ready projects that can begin construction by next spring.

The third stream, innovation, will offer funding for organizations and unions with ideas to recruit, retain and train Red Seal trades, including supporting apprentices in progressing toward certification.
This could include things like integrating artificial intelligence or helping recruit apprentices through new initiatives.
Part of $6B plan for workers
The formal announcement is set to take place on Thursday morning in Metcalfe, Ont., just outside of Ottawa.
In the 2026 spring economic update, the federal government pledged $6 billion over five years to recruit, train and hire workers.

items: Ottawa's $6B recruitment push not enough to get Manitobans into trades: colleges
Billions more for defence, but Canada's military still faces an old budget squeeze

blocks.text: It announced plans to offer wage subsidies for employers that hire apprentices, creating paid, entry-level trades-related work that leads to apprenticeship and offering apprentices with a weekly income top-up, as well as training completion bonuses.
The details of those plans — including when they are set to be rolled out — have not yet been released.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New
The RCMP, Royal Newfoundland Constabulary, Newfoundland Power and City of St. John's are some organizations who say their phones lines are affected by the widespread Bell outage.
The cause of the outage is not known
A widespread Bell telecommunications outage is affecting calls in Newfoundland and Labrador, including some people trying to call 911 and other non-emergency police phone lines.
In a social media post, Bell Aliant said customers may not be able to make voice calls, including to emergency services.

"We are working to restore service as quickly as possible. If you require emergency assistance, please go directly to the nearest fire station, police station or hospital emergency department," reads the statement.
The Royal Newfoundland Constabulary says its non-emergency telephone reporting line is unavailable, but says its 911 system isn't affected.
Newfoundland Power is also affected.
"Customer service and emergency phone lines are currently unavailable," reads a social media post from the utility.
Newfoundland Power says people can call 709-685-5078 for power outages, downed lines, or other electricity system emergencies only.
The City of St. John's says its 311 service is not available to Bell customers, either.

articles.title: Injured victim dies following crash at B.C. mall on Truth and Reconciliation Day: police
articles.summary: Delta police say the cause of the vehicle crash at Tsawwassen Mills mall on Sept. 30 remains under investigation.

image.caption: Flowers at the scene of the fatal collision at Tsawwassen Mills mall on Sept. 30. (Georgie Smyth/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Delta police say the cause of the vehicle crash at Tsawwassen Mills mall on Sept. 30 remains under investigation.
Police say cause of Sept. 30 collision remains under investigation
Delta police say another victim has died as a result of the vehicle crash at Tsawwassen Mills mall on Sept. 30.
Police said in a news release Tuesday that 64-year-old Gwenyth Brigit Dwyn of South Delta, one of two people who were hospitalized following the crash, has died as a result of her injuries.
Two other people were declared dead at the scene, where a house pole raising event had been taking place following a Truth and Reconciliation Day walk hosted by Tsawwassen First Nation.
Police initially said the vehicle's driver "may have experienced a medical emergency," but added Wednesday that investigators have not reached any final conclusions on the cause of the crash.

items: 2 elders from Tsawwassen First Nation killed in crash at Truth and Reconciliation Day event

blocks.text: The two people killed at the scene were Tsawwassen First Nation elders Virginia Splockton and wilapiya (Barb Joe).
Police said Wednesday the second injured person has been released from hospital and continues their recovery at home.
"Our thoughts remain with the victims families and loved ones, and with everyone affected by this tragedy," Delta police said.
Cause remains under investigation
The department has faced criticism over a lack of public updates on the investigation. Before Wednesday, there had not been an update since Oct. 1.

items: More updates from police needed on TRC day fatal collision investigation, says law professor

blocks.text: In their new statement, Delta police Staff Sgt. Mike Whiteley said the responsibility of police is to ensure answers are based on an objective examination of evidence.
"Investigators are working through a significant amount of information, and it is important that we not reach conclusions before that work is complete."
First responders outside the mall after the collision. (Johna Baylon/CBC)
The release said investigators have reviewed a "substantial volume of evidence including cellphone and other video evidence," and completed a scene and collision analysis.

"This work includes examining the movements of the involved vehicle on the Tsawwassen Mills property before the pedestrians were struck, including an earlier collision. Investigators have not reached any final conclusions regarding the cause of the collisions," Delta police said.
"Based on the evidence reviewed to date, investigators have not identified evidence indicating that the collision was targeted or ideologically motivated."
Police said they continue to investigate the "possibility that the driver experienced a medical event prior to the collisions."
Anyone who witnessed the incident or who observed the vehicle on the mall property before the crash, and has not already spoken to investigators, is asked to contact Delta police.

articles.title: SpaceX rocket launch causes stunning ‘jellyfish cloud’ visible off US east coast
articles.summary:
Expanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalized in the sky and reflected sunlight off frozen particles after Florida launch

A SpaceX…

blocks.text: A SpaceX rocket provided a stunning pre-dawn display over Florida as a massive, luminescent “jellyfish cloud” spread for miles, caused by an expanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalizing in the sky and reflecting sunlight off the frozen particles.
The phenomenon occurred shortly after Tuesday’s 6.33am ET launch of the Falcon 9 rocket carrying cargo to the International Space Station.

The timing of the blastoff, 48 minutes before sunrise at Florida’s Cape Canaveral space force station, provided a perfect example of the colorful effect only fully visible from Earth during dusk and dawn launches.
The rocket’s north-eastern trajectory over the Atlantic also allowed residents of eastern states from Georgia to New York to enjoy the spectacle.

Nasa posted photographs of the jellyfish cloud on X, the social media platform owned by SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk. Among the hundreds of replies were images taken by sky watchers across multiple states.

Those who missed Tuesday’s dazzling celestial show have another opportunity to view one next Monday, 19 October, when another SpaceX Falcon 9 is scheduled to lift off from the same space force station pad.
An hour-long launch window for the satellite-deployment mission opens at 6.30am ET, little more than a half hour before the 7.01am sunrise.

articles.title: Nord Stream trial opens in Germany, defense seeks dismissal
articles.summary: Serhii Kuznietsov is accused of attacking civilian infrastructure in the 2022 sabotage of the Russian gas pipeline to Germany. His lawyers called Nord Stream a military target, and said their client…

image.caption: Serhii Kuznietsov's defense team argued that the alleged actions should not be deemed a criminal actImage: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The trial of a former Ukrainian special forces officer, Serhii Kuznietsov, opened in the northern German city of Hamburg on Wednesday amid considerable public and press interest.

Kuznietsov is accused of leading the September 2022 sabotage operation that put the undersea Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines linking Russian to Germany out of action. The pipelines remain inactive four years later, with no sign of plans to ever reactivate them as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine heads into its fifth winter.

Prosecutors accuse the Ukrainian of participation in a war crime by targeting civilian infrastructure, but his defense lawyers on Wednesday argued that the case should be dismissed entirely on multiple grounds.

blocks.caption: The defense lawyers argue that the case should be thrown out entirely, saying their client is forbidden from speaking with them or anybody else about the caseImage: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Kuznietsov's lawyers say on opening day?
A team of three lawyers representing Kuznietsov questioned the premise of the trial in court.
One of Kuznietsov's lawyers, Nicola Canestrini, argued that it was not valid to try the officer on war crimes charges for an attack on civilian infrastructure.

He argued that the pipeline, which provided half of Germany's natural gas imports prior to Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, was ultimately a "Russian weapon," given the importance of energy revenues for funding Moscow's military.
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked the court.
After the charges were read out, the judge asked Kuznietsov if he wanted to comment, and he said that he did not.
His lawyers argue that this silence extends beyond not speaking in court and say this should be the main grounds for dismissal.
They say Kuznietsov is sworn to secrecy by his home government in Ukraine and so is unable to discuss his case or potential exonerating evidence with anyone, including his legal representatives.

"He is not permitted to speak. His two immediate superiors told him that he does not have authorization to make any statements — not even to his lawyers," defense attorney Jes Meyer-Lohkamp told the court. In German law, Meyer-Lohkamp argued: "Anyone who cannot speak out cannot be convicted."

blocks.caption: A small group of demonstrators stood outside the court on Wednesday arguing that the wrong party to the war in Ukraine was on trialImage: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What was the mood in court in Hamburg?
DW's Matthew Moore was on hand in the court in northern Germany on Wednesday.
There is huge interest in this court case, Moore reported. No sooner had the court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg than the first journalists, observers and protesters began arriving.

A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told Moore they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."
Inside, a Ukrainian student told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.

"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero," the student said. In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.

blocks.caption: Based on investigative reporting and a Bojan Pancevski book on the sabotage published this year, Kuznietsov coordinated a small and unlikely team made up not of professional spies or soldiers, but rather people with relevant specialist skills like deep-sea divers and explosives expertsImage: Mark…

blocks.text: Geramny's Wadephul: 'We will deal with any outcome'
The case has been highly politically awkward for Germany — a staunch supporter of Ukraine despite investigators pursuing a trail that led to Kuznietsov and other suspects.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly denied any Ukrainian involvement in the operation, and had also resisted Kuznietsov's extradition to Germany after his arrest in Italy last year, arguing that there was no case to answer.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul declined to comment on the trial on Wednesday, saying that the most important thing for now was for the case to proceed with no political interference or restrictions.
"We will deal with any outcome, and we will, of course, take it into account in our political calculations," he told a press conference in Berlin.
Court dates for the trial are currently scheduled through February of next year but this could be subject to change in either direction.
With additional reporting from DW's Matthew Moore in Hamburg.

articles.title: How Trump’s diesel deal with Russia will impact the United States and Ukraine
articles.summary: US President Trump’s diesel deal with Russia has alarmed Ukraine and its allies. What is he hoping to achieve at home, and what does the deal mean for Kyiv and Moscow?

image.caption: Donald Trump now allows Russian diesel imports into the USImage: Eric Lee/REUTERS

blocks.text: Many Ukrainians and Europeans viewed news from Washington over the past weekend as a stab in the back by their US ally. First, President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, which involves a temporary easing of US sanctions against Moscow.

And later Trump announced an allegedly agreed "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia. Kyiv said the idea had not been discussed with Ukraine, but that it was prepared to halt attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure if Moscow did the same.
'Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine'

Security expert Carlo Masala of the Bundeswehr University Munich said the developments showed that "Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine at all, but that domestic US politics and relations with Russia are far more important to him than supporting Ukraine."
He added that the president aims to sway the outcome of the US midterm elections on November 3 through an agreement with Russia.

All seats in the House of Representatives and a regularly scheduled portion of the Senate will be contested in the midterm elections. Polls suggest that Trump's Republican Party could lose its majority in the House. A loss of the Republicans' Senate majority is also possible. Surveys indicate that American voters are unhappy with high fuel prices, and the US president apparently hopes to influence prices through diesel shipments from Russia.
Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices?
Observers, however, consider Trump's hopes that Russian diesel shipments could affect prices in the US illusory.
"The volume is so small that it will have absolutely no effect on prices," Thomas Jäger of the University of Cologne told German public broadcaster ARD.
The political scientist added that shipments planned before the midterm elections would not even cover US diesel demand for a single day.
"The same applies to any shipments that may arrive afterward, if they materialize, they will have no effect on prices either," he said.
Trump's goal, Jäger said, is simply "the story" — showing voters that he is trying to solve a problem that matters to them.
'No concrete military benefits for Russia'
The main criticism from Kyiv and EU countries is that Russia will use the revenue from diesel sales to finance its war against Ukraine.
Carlo Masala, however, does not foresee the agreement with the US having "any concrete positive military effects" for Russia.
He points out that Washington had already temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian oil exports in March this year, shortly after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran.

"Despite the money Russia has and has received, it has no military strategy for making further advances in the Donbas. The issue is more about the political impact and the symbolism of the Americans striking separate deals with the Russians at Ukraine's expense," the expert said.

Another cause for concern in Kyiv could be US threats to suspend intelligence sharing with Ukraine and block the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) program unless Ukraine halts its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Under the PURL program, European countries procure US weapons for Ukraine.
Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?
European alternatives to US intelligence

A possible US decision to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine for strikes on Russian territory would have "dramatic" consequences for Kyiv, Masala said, but European intelligence, particularly from France, could help mitigate the impact.
While French intelligence is "not as comprehensive as American intelligence," the Ukrainian military already uses it to carry out strikes in Russia with French weapons systems.

As for the weapons European countries procure from the US for Ukraine under the PURL program, Masala noted that the program's most important component — interceptor missiles for air defense — has barely been available to Ukraine since the start of the war with Iran.
Support for Ukraine across both US parties

Ahead of the US midterm elections, experts point out that Ukraine enjoys broad support not only among Democrats but also among Republicans. One example is the bipartisan passage this summer of legislation to tighten US sanctions against Russia, known as the "Lindsey Graham Act," named after its Republican congressional sponsor, who has since died.

Signed by Trump in September, the law gives the president a broad range of tools. He can impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and Russia's shadow fleet, which is used to circumvent restrictions on oil exports. He can also impose punitive tariffs on buyers of Russian energy products.

blocks.caption: There is broad bipartisan support for Ukraine in US CongressImage: Valerio Rosati/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Trump may resist, but political forces, particularly after the US midterms, may push the administration in the direction of trying to seek an end to the war by using the tools available," former US diplomat Daniel Fried told DW.

He added that the "Lindsey Graham Act" and the 2022 law banning US imports of Russian oil are "not absolute, but strong barriers against dumb ideas like a unilateral unrequited diesel deal with Russia."

Several Democratic and Republican senators cited this legislation in a joint statement in which they described the diesel deal with Russia as illegal, calling on the US government to "immediately correct" its decision.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian

articles.title: Mournful elephant mom wins 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year
articles.summary: An Italian photographer's "heartbreakingly poignant" photo of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won this year's top Wildlife Photographer of the Year award. See a selection of the other…

blocks.text: Science·Photos

An Italian photographer's "heartbreakingly poignant" photo of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won this year's top Wildlife Photographer of the Year award. See a selection of the other winning photos here.
Youth award goes to photo of hard-working dung beetle
(Federico Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)
An Italian photographer's "heartbreakingly poignant" photo of a mother elephant carrying her dead calf has won this year's top Wildlife Photographer of the Year award.

Federico Veronesi captured "The Aftermath" while tracking elephants in the Huab River Valley in Namibia. He noticed unusual drag marks in the sand of the dry riverbed. When he caught up to a family of elephants, he saw an adult female with a calf's leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.
Kathy Moran, chair of the jury for the 2026 competition, described the photo as working on "so many levels."
"Emotionally it's a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant. Intellectually, it's proof that animals have cognition," she wrote in a news release announcing the winners.
In addition to winning the grand prize, the photo also won the Behaviour: Mammals category.

Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the U.K.-based Natural History Museum in London, with a stated goal to share nature's stories and insights about environmental challenges that need our attention.
This year, the annual competition — the 62nd edition — attracted 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories.
It awards top prizes to both an adult photographer and a young photographer under 18.
This year's Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year prize was won by Oscar Whitfield, a young British photographer who grew up in Zimbabwe and frequently returns there during school holidays.
His photo, captured while lying on the ground, shows a close-up of a dung beetle hard at work pushing a ball of dung. It was also the winner in the 11 to 14 years age bracket.
(Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the year)

Officially, there were no Canadian category winners this year. However, Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, who lives in Germany and won this year's Rising Star Award, is a Canadian citizen who has previously told CBC News his parents were both born in Canada, and he has relatives in Ottawa and Nova Scotia.

His featured photo, "Afternoon snack," is a close-up of a robber fly preying on a flesh fly. "The bubbles forming in the victim's eyes indicate that the robber fly has injected digestive enzymes that liquefy its internal tissues before they are sucked out," the photo's description reads.
(Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)
Canadians can see the 100-photo exhibition at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto from Nov 7, 2026, to Feb 28, 2027.
It opens at the Natural History Museum in London this Friday.
Here are some of the other category winners.
Amelie Davis, of the U.K., won the 10 years and under bracket with this photo of a common carder bee in southern England, captured with her father's smartphone.
(Amelie Davis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

A California newt lays eggs while clasping vegetation that already contains another newt's egg clutch in the winner of the Amphibians and Reptiles category, captured by U.S. photographer Anton Sorokin. The newt will stay like this until the egg mass swells to a size too large to be eaten by a predator.
(Anton Sorokin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

Greek photographer Agorastos Papatsanis used UV light to make these fluorescent bonnet mushrooms glow brightly on a decaying log on the lower slopes of Greece's Mount Olympus. The image won the Plants and Fungi category.
(Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

A young bull elephant sprays water on a group of zebras at a waterhole in the Chyulu Hills of Kenya in this photo, the winner of the Animals in their Environment category, captured by James Lewin using a camera converted to infrared to soften harsh lighting.
(James Lewin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year)

articles.title: Southern California beach closes after sighting of great white shark ‘exhibiting aggressive behavior’
articles.summary:
Two-mile stretch of Huntington Beach closed after sighting at location popular with surfers and swimmers

A popular southern

blocks.text: A popular southern California beach was closed after a great white shark was reportedly spotted “exhibiting aggressive behavior” on Tuesday afternoon.

The Huntington Beach fire department said there was a “credible report” of a 10-12ft great white shark circling near a lifeguard tower, which is considered aggressive behavior according to the city’s marine safety division’s “shark response protocols”.

Officials closed a two-mile long stretch of beach near the tower between Seapoint and the Huntington Beach pier through Wednesday afternoon, and said workers had posted warning signs and notified visitors.
“Please follow all posted signs and instructions from lifeguards. Public safety remains our top priority,” the city’s fire department said in a statement.
The Orange county beach is popular with surfers and swimmers.
California saw an unusually high number of great white sharks over the summer as juveniles fled warm waters in Mexico amid El Niño. Experts said humans shouldn’t be alarmed.

Shark incidents involving bites are “extremely rare” in California, according to the state’s department of fish and wildlife. There have been fewer than 250 shark incidents in the state since 1950, and fewer than 20 were fatal.

Scientists agree that such incidents are generally “exploratory bites” as a result of sharks investigating “unusual objects in their environment, such as kayaks”, the fish and wildlife department said.
